Using the linearity property of double integrals, we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A-{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A+{∬}_{R}\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the first integral is independent of $y.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}{x}^{2}\text{ }\text{d}A & =(4-0){\int }_{-3}^{0}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]_{-3}^{0} \\  & =4(\frac{{0}^{3}}{3}-\frac{(-3)^{3}}{3}) \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

The function under the second integral is independent of $x.$ So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}y\text{ }\text{d}A & =(0-(-3)){\int }_{0}^{4}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =3[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]_{0}^{4} \\  & =3(\frac{{4}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}) \\  & =24.\end{aligned}
$$

The third integral is the double integral of unity:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}\text{d}A=\text{Area}(R)=3\cdot 4=12\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, combining our results, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{R}({x}^{2}-y+1)\,\text{d}A=36-24+12=24.\end{aligned}
$$
